title: How to Read an Income Statement as an Investor
summary: How to read an income statement from revenue to net income: what each line means, which margins and changes to check first, and what the statement cannot tell you about cash.
body_markdown:
The SEC guide puts it plainly: an income statement can tell you whether a company made a profit, and a cash-flow statement can tell you whether it generated cash. The two are related but not equivalent, and no one financial statement tells the complete story. Pair it with the[balance sheet](https://meetbenson.com/blog/how-to-read-a-balance-sheet/) to see what the company owes and owns at the end of the period.


There is also no single good margin. The SEC notes that desirable ratios vary by industry, so compare a company with its own earlier filings and with competitors' filings rather than with a rule of thumb. EPS is the link to valuation: the SEC's example of a $20 share price and $2 of EPS gives a P/E of 10, meaning the stock sells at 10 times earnings. That is a description of the price, not a judgment on whether it is right.
